Expected Utility and Risk Attitudes

The EV analyses treat tokens as though participants were indifferent to risk. A participant who dislikes risk could reasonably prefer the sportsbook favorite, which always had the smaller payoff SD, even when the sportsbook underdog had the higher EV. To test whether risk attitudes could account for the departures from EV maximization, we fit a one-parameter expected utility (EU) model to each participant’s bets. We used a constant absolute risk aversion (CARA) utility function, u(x) = (1 - e-θx)/θ, where x is the outcome of a bet measured in stakes (one stake is the participant’s mean number of tokens per bet) and θ is the participant’s risk attitude: θ > 0 indicates risk aversion, θ < 0 indicates risk seeking, and θ = 0 indicates risk neutrality, in which case EU equals EV (details in Appendix A). Because participants made two decisions in every match, whether to bet on the match and which team to bet on, we estimated θ separately from each decision, which allowed us to test whether a single utility curve could describe both. These analyses include participants who bet at least one token (R16: n = 496; QF: n = 496) and pool the odds conditions.

Model. Consider a bet of one stake on a team the participant gives probability p of advancing, with profit b stakes per stake wagered (b = profit/100 from the American odds). The bet ends at +b with probability p and at -1 with probability 1 - p; not betting ends at 0. A participant’s utility of an outcome x (in stakes) is

\[u(x) = \frac{1 - e^{-\theta x}}{\theta} \quad (\theta \neq 0), \qquad u(x) = x \quad (\theta = 0),\]

so the expected utility of the bet and its certainty equivalent (the sure amount, in stakes, valued the same as the bet) are

\[EU(\theta; p, b) = p\,u(b) + (1 - p)\,u(-1), \qquad CE(\theta; p, b) = u^{-1}\!\left(EU\right) = -\frac{1}{\theta}\ln\!\left[p\,e^{-\theta b} + (1 - p)\,e^{\theta}\right],\]

with \(CE \to pb - (1 - p) = EV\) as \(\theta \to 0\). A participant prefers the bet to not betting if and only if \(CE > 0\), which holds if and only if \(\theta < \theta^*\), where the break-even risk attitude \(\theta^*\) solves \(p\,e^{-\theta^* b} + (1 - p)\,e^{\theta^*} = 1\). The break-even is positive when the bet has a positive EV and negative when it has a negative EV. Risk attitude per stake is θ = αS, where α is the absolute risk aversion per token and S is the participant’s mean tokens per bet; the sign of θ, and therefore every classification below, does not depend on S. Each participant has one θ, estimated from their own bets and held fixed across matches (the other parameters, p and b, come from the participant’s stated probability and the match’s odds).

Decision 1: whether to bet. Each match offers two bets, one on each team. The participant bets on match m if the better of the two has a positive certainty equivalent, that is, if

\[\theta < \theta^*_m = \max\left(\theta^*_{m,\text{fav}},\ \theta^*_{m,\text{dog}}\right),\]

where fav and dog are the sportsbook favorite and underdog. Ordering the M break-even values from largest to smallest, \(\theta^*_{(1)} \geq \dots \geq \theta^*_{(M)}\), a participant who bet on exactly k matches must have

\[\theta^*_{(k+1)} \leq \theta < \theta^*_{(k)},\]

which is an interval for θ (an upper bound only if k = M, and a lower bound only if k = 0). We report the value in the interval closest to 0. Because the interval is built from the number of bets, EU reproduces it by construction, and the only way for this decision to fail is for the interval to be empty (a team given a 100% chance of advancing that the participant did not bet on).

Decision 2: which team to bet on. In matches in which the participant bet, the participant chooses the sportsbook favorite if \(CE_{\text{fav}}(\theta) > CE_{\text{dog}}(\theta)\) and the underdog otherwise, which is a different restriction on θ: risk aversion moves the choice toward the bet with the smaller payoff SD and, at high levels, toward the team more likely to advance, and risk seeking moves it toward the underdog. We estimate θ as the value on a grid (-4 to 4 by .01, plus ±30) that maximizes the share of the participant’s team choices it reproduces, using matches with at least one token bet and excluding the U.S.-Belgium 50% estimates (identical bets). Ties go to the value closest to 0.

Both decisions with one utility function. Expected utility theory assigns each participant one utility function, so the same θ must satisfy both restrictions. We tested this by (a) classifying θ from each decision separately (Table 13), (b) asking whether a θ in the participant’s number-of-bets interval also fits their team choices as well as any θ does, (c) predicting each decision with the θ estimated from the other (Table 15), and (d) fitting one θ to the three-way outcome in each match (no bet, sportsbook favorite, sportsbook underdog) and cross-validating it by leaving out one match at a time (Table 14). Whether to bet alone is not a test of the model, because it reproduces the number of bets by construction and, when a participant bet on every match, bounds θ from only one side. Which team to bet on is the decision on which the EV analyses departed from risk neutrality, so it is the decision a risk attitude must account for.

Risk attitudes implied by whether to bet. Participants bet on most matches (R16: M = 6.5 of 8; QF: M = 3.8 of 4), including matches in which both teams had a negative EV given the participant’s own probability (13.4% of R16 bets and 9.9% of QF bets), which only a risk-seeking participant would accept. The number of bets implied risk seeking for 39.7% of participants in R16 and 29.0% in QF, risk aversion for 29.8% and 9.5%, and was consistent with risk neutrality for 28.4% and 60.7% (Table 13). No risk attitude reproduced the number of bets for 10 R16 and 4 QF participants, who gave a team a 100% chance of advancing but did not bet on that match. The implied risk attitudes were close to risk neutrality (R16: Mdn = .00, IQR [-.08, .08]; QF: Mdn = .00, IQR [-.03, .00]) because most bets had EVs near zero, so a small change in risk attitude was enough to change whether a bet was worth taking. With θ set to reproduce each participant’s number of bets, EU correctly identified whether a match was bet on in 87.2% of R16 and 95.9% of QF matches (80.6% and 86.9% when each match was predicted from the participant’s other matches), compared with 73.2% and 85.4% for EV (betting whenever either team had a positive EV; Table 14).

Risk attitudes implied by which team to bet on. Team choices implied risk aversion for 50.2% of participants in R16 and 42.9% in QF, risk seeking for 8.5% and 8.5%, and were consistent with risk neutrality for 40.1% and 46.8%. The median risk-averse participant (R16: θ = .53; QF: θ = .63) would value a 50/50 bet to win or lose one stake at -.25 and -.30 stakes, that is, would give up about a quarter of a stake to avoid it. EU with each participant’s θ predicted the team bet on in 86.3% of R16 and 87.8% of QF bets (76.3% and 72.8% cross-validated), compared with 68.8% and 65.9% for EV (Table 14).

One utility curve for both decisions. The two decisions implied different risk attitudes (Table 13 and Figure 4). Of participants whose number of bets implied risk seeking, 64.0% in R16 and 53.5% in QF chose teams in a way that implied risk aversion. Risk attitudes estimated from team choices were higher (more risk averse) than those estimated from the number of bets (Wilcoxon signed-rank test; R16: z = 6.16, p < .001; QF: z = Inf, p < .001), and the two estimates were negatively correlated in R16 (rs = -.21, p < .001) and unrelated in QF (rs = -.06, p = .214). When a single θ was fit to both decisions, EU predicted 55.2% of R16 and 57.2% of QF decisions (no bet, sportsbook favorite, or sportsbook underdog) cross-validated, compared with 49.1% and 55.4% for EV (Table 14). Risk attitudes implied by team choices did not differ by odds condition (R16: p = .213; QF: p = .521), whereas risk attitudes implied by the number of bets were lower (more risk seeking) for anchored than unanchored participants in both samples (R16: p = .032; QF: p = .033; Wilcoxon rank-sum tests).

Is whether to bet enough? Modeling only whether to bet, which was our starting point, has three limits in these data. First, EU reproduces each participant’s number of bets by construction, so a high fit is not evidence for the model. Second, it identifies θ from one side only for participants who bet on every match (R16: 58.1%; QF: 88.5%), who are told only that θ is below some value, which is why so many are classified as risk neutral or risk seeking. Third, it makes no prediction about the decision on which the EV analyses departed from risk neutrality. Setting θ to the value implied by the number of bets did not improve prediction of team choices over EV (R16: 66.7% vs. 68.8%; QF: 62.1% vs. 65.9%), and setting θ to the value implied by team choices predicted whether to bet worse than EV (R16: 50.5% vs. 73.2%; QF: 60.6% vs. 85.4%; Table 15). Only 43.3% of R16 and 50.4% of QF participants had a θ consistent with their number of bets that also fit their team choices as well as any θ did. We therefore report both decisions: the number of bets is the decision for which the EU model was originally proposed, and team choice is the decision that gives it something to explain.

Thus, a single utility curve could not describe both decisions. Participants bet on nearly every match, as a risk-neutral or risk-seeking bettor would, but chose which team to bet on as a risk-averse bettor would. The risk aversion implied by team choices mirrors the preference for the participant favorite: for a highly risk-averse bettor, the better bet is the team more likely to advance, which in discordant matches was also the sportsbook favorite with the smaller payoff SD. A preference for betting on the team expected to advance therefore accounts for both decisions more simply than a stable attitude toward risk.

Appendix A: Statistical Details

Interpreting American odds. American odds express profit relative to the stake, excluding the return of the stake. Negative odds (e.g., -140) mark the favorite: a 140-token bet returns 100 tokens of profit. Positive odds (e.g., +130) mark the underdog: a 100-token bet returns 130 tokens of profit. Implied probability = |odds| / (|odds| + 100) for negative odds and 100 / (odds + 100) for positive odds. The two teams’ implied probabilities sum to more than 1 (the vig); sportsbook probabilities in the analyses divide each team’s implied probability by the two teams’ sum. In each match the sportsbook favorite is the team with the lower American odds; the U.S. is treated as the sportsbook favorite against Belgium (both -110), so the U.S. and Belgium are each .50. EV per 100 tokens from the participant’s own stated probability p: EV = p x (100 + profit) - 100, where profit = 100 x 100/|odds| for negative odds and equals the odds for positive odds.

Odds conditions and favorites. Early Odds (data label “American Odds Condition”) = anchored, odds shown while predicting; Late Odds (“No Odds Condition”) = unanchored, odds shown only when betting. Sections 1 and 2 compare the conditions; Sections 3 and 4 pool them. The participant favorite is the team the participant predicted to advance (Block 1 pick); the sportsbook favorite is defined above.

Probability estimates and anchoring. Per-match Welch t-tests compare the probability anchored and unanchored participants assigned to the sportsbook favorite (the underdog’s is its complement); Holm correction across the 12 matches; d with pooled SD. Deviation = participant probability for the sportsbook favorite - sportsbook probability, in percentage points. Condition differences in absolute and signed deviation use linear mixed models, and the share of estimates within 2 points uses a logistic mixed model, all with match fixed effects and a participant random intercept. The share of participant favorites that were the sportsbook favorite is compared by logistic mixed models (participant random intercept), overall and by match outcome. The scatterplot (Appendix C) shows participant vs. sportsbook probability with linear fits; the slope difference is the sportsbook x condition interaction in a linear mixed model (participant random intercept; Satterthwaite df).

Brier scores. A participant’s Brier score is the mean over matches of the squared difference between the probability assigned to a team and the outcome (1 if it advanced, 0 otherwise). Within a match, the mean individual Brier score equals (mean probability - outcome)^2 + variance of probabilities across participants: collective error + dispersion (Krogh & Vedelsby, 1994). Exact; no probability bins; invariant to which team is labeled the event. 95% CIs from a cluster bootstrap (2,000 resamples of participants, keeping each participant’s matches together). Condition differences in mean Brier score use Welch t-tests. Reference strategies: always 50/50; always back the sportsbook favorite with certainty (U.S. counted as the favorite); the de-vigged sportsbook probability. Correlations: Pearson, mean Brier score with final tokens and number of bets won.

Expected value analyses. Team-level rows (mean EV, % positive) use participant x team evaluations with team fixed effects; match-level rows use participant x match observations with match fixed effects; all have a participant random intercept (linear for EV, logistic for percentages). Higher-EV team = team with the larger EV from the participant’s own probability; estimates with equal EVs (50% for the U.S. at -110/-110) are excluded. Discordant match = the participant favorite is not the higher-EV team.

Repeated-measures correlations. Each variable is centered within participant and the centered values are pooled (Bakdash & Marusich, 2017); df = observations - participants - 1. Correlations with binary variables are point-biserial. Holm correction across the 15 pairs within each sample. R16 below the diagonal, QF above.

Models of betting on the sportsbook favorite. Outcome = Block 3 bet on the sportsbook favorite (1) vs. underdog (0). Mixed-effects logistic regressions (glmer) with a participant random intercept; continuous predictors standardized within sample. Payoff SD of a 100-token bet = (profit + 100) x sqrt(p(1 - p)). The combined model replaces the probability with the binary participant favorite = sportsbook favorite (less collinear with the EV difference) and adds odds condition as a covariate; VIFs from linear regressions among the predictors. Relative importance = general dominance weights (Luo & Azen, 2013) on marginal R2 (Nakagawa & Schielzeth, 2013; fixed-effect variance / (fixed + random-intercept + pi^2/3)), over all subsets of the five predictors, reported as % of the full-model marginal R2. % classified from the fixed effects only (log-odds > 0).

Bet distribution profiles. Normalized HHI = (HHI - 1/k)/(1 - 1/k), k = 8 (R16) or 4 (QF); participants who wagered no tokens are excluded. Strategy value = normalized HHI of half the tokens on one match and the rest spread evenly. Within each sample, bettors were split 80/20 (seeded) into training and testing sets; normalized HHI and proportion of matches bet on were standardized with training moments; k-means (50-100 starts) for k = 2 to 6; k = 3 chosen from variance explained and average silhouette width. A depth-3 CART tree (minimum node size 15) fitted to the training clusters gives threshold rules, evaluated in the testing set and then applied to all bettors. Stability = mean Jaccard similarity of each training cluster across 200 bootstrap re-clusterings (Hennig, 2007). Group differences use one-way ANOVAs (partial eta-squared) and Games-Howell post hoc tests.

Tokens on the participant favorite vs. the higher-EV team. Option A: discordant matches with a bet of at least one token; tokens per bet compared between bets on the participant favorite and on the higher-EV team with a linear mixed model (participant random intercept). Option B: per participant, total tokens on participant favorites and on higher-EV teams across all matches, compared with a paired t-test. Both use the final bet and token amount; matches with equal EVs are excluded.

Expected utility analyses. Equations for the utility function, certainty equivalent, break-even risk attitude, and the two decision rules are given in the Expected Utility and Risk Attitudes section. Utility is constant absolute risk aversion (CARA), u(x) = (1 - exp(-theta x))/theta (u(x) = x when theta = 0), where x is the outcome of a bet in stakes and one stake is the participant’s mean tokens per bet among matches with a bet. A bet on a team with stated probability p at odds paying b tokens of profit per token wagered wins b stakes with probability p and loses one stake otherwise, so its certainty equivalent is CE = -(1/theta) ln[p exp(-theta b) + (1 - p) exp(theta)]. CARA was used because it does not depend on the participant’s token balance, so each match can be evaluated separately, and because it nests EV (theta = 0). The stake only rescales theta (risk aversion per token = theta / stake), so the sign of every estimate, and therefore every classification, is the same for any stake. For each bet, the break-even risk attitude theta* solves CE = 0 (theta* > 0 for positive-EV bets and < 0 for negative-EV bets), and a bet is worth taking whenever theta < theta. Whether to bet:* a match’s break-even value is the larger of its two teams’ theta; a participant who bet on k of M matches has theta between the (k + 1)th and kth largest break-even values, and the predicted matches are the k with the largest break-even values. Which team to bet on:* the predicted team has the larger CE at theta; theta was chosen on a grid (-4 to 4 in steps of .01, plus -30 and 30) to maximize the percentage of bets on the predicted team, using matches with a bet of at least one token (final team) and excluding the U.S. vs. Belgium estimates of exactly 50%, for which the two bets are identical. Both decisions: one theta chosen to maximize the percentage of matches with the correct decision (no bet, sportsbook favorite, or sportsbook underdog). When several values fit equally well, the value closest to 0 was used. A participant was classified as consistent with risk neutrality when theta = 0 was among the best-fitting values, as risk averse when all best-fitting values were positive, and as risk seeking when all were negative. Cross-validated accuracy predicts each match from theta estimated on the participant’s other matches (leave one match out). Risk attitudes from the two decisions were compared with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and Spearman correlations, and between odds conditions with Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. The model assumes that stated probabilities are participants’ beliefs, that matches are evaluated independently, and that every bet is the same size, and it does not model the bonus rule (only tokens above 100 were paid), which rewards risk taking.
